own_scenes.desc: En 1966 las mujeres seguían siendo ciudadanas de segunda: leyes duras sobre divorcio y aborto, una mujer británica no podía abrir una cuenta sin su marido, los anuncios de empleo separaban empleos con futuro (hombres) y sin salida (mujeres). Pero el pleno empleo, la píldora (desde 1961), las familias más pequeñas y los electrodomésticos lo estaban cambiando. Betty Friedan dio nombre en The Feminine Mystique (1963) al «problema sin nombre» de las amas de casa de los suburbios, deprimidas y medicadas; Simone de Beauvoir (El segundo sexo, 1949) fue la piedra de toque de las jóvenes británicas como Sheila Rowbotham; Nell Dunn recogió en Talking to Women la búsqueda de realización personal. Llegaron la Equal Pay Act (1963), el título VII de la Ley de Derechos Civiles (1964) y Barbara Castle como primera ministra. Casey Hayden y Mary King, voluntarias del SNCC en el Freedom Summer, escribieron «A Kind of Memo» sobre el «sistema de castas sexual» incluso dentro del movimiento; en diciembre de 1965 las mujeres del SDS se reunieron aparte y en abril de 1966 Liberation publicó el manifiesto entero. La segunda ola aún no había empezado, pero algo estaba en el aire.

notes.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro
notes.text: El 29 de octubre se presentó en Washington la National Organization for Women de Betty Friedan, con trescientas socias: pasar de la discusión a la acción contra la «cortina de seda» de los prejuicios, la falta de mujeres en la dirección de empresas y gobierno y la imagen falsa de la mujer en los medios. El best seller del año, Valley of the Dolls, hablaba de dependencia femenina y pastillas; la serie That Girl mostraba a una actriz que vivía sola; «Born a Woman» de Sandy Posey oscilaba entre el desafío y la sumisión.

refs.q: In 1966, women were still treated as second-class citizens.
refs.para: In 1966, women were still treated as second-class citizens. Both in America and the UK, there were stringent laws about divorce and abortion. In the UK, family law still allowed husbands considerable control over their wives: for instance, a woman could not open a bank account without the approval of her spouse. Women were subject to inequalities in employment, both in pay and the nature of the jobs available. They also bore the brunt of the social disapproval resulting from any sexual activity outside marriage.

refs.q: Many of the ideas and attitudes in Talking to Women could have come straight out of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique.
refs.para: Many of the ideas and attitudes in Talking to Women could have come straight out of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique. Published in 1963, this groundbreaking polemic had a huge impact at the time, focusing its ideas with enough clarity and force to start a political movement. Much of Friedan’s book reads like the theoretical underpinning for the first three series of Mad Men, set in the early sixties, with Betty Draper as the listless suburban wife driven mad by an all-pervading yet nameless anomie.

refs.q: This was an idea that had found its time.
refs.para: The response was immediate. In December 1965, inspired by the memo, female attendees of a Students for a Democratic Society convention in Illinois walked out and held a separate meeting of what they called ‘A Women’s Caucus’. A few months later, in April 1966, the War Resisters League magazine, Liberation, printed the manifesto in full – a publication that, according to King, ‘increased by a quantum leap the number of people circulating it’. This was an idea that had found its time.

refs.q: On 29 October, the three hundred members of NOW – professionals all – agreed the full Statement of Purpose.
refs.para: On 29 October, the three hundred members of NOW – professionals all – agreed the full Statement of Purpose. It began with a simple statement: ‘We believe the time has come to move beyond the abstract argument, discussion and symposia over the status and special nature of women which has raged in America in recent years; the time has come to confront, with concrete action, the conditions that now prevent women from enjoying the equality of opportunity and freedom of choice which is their right, as individual Americans, and as human beings.’
